sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to the Runaway Feedback Loop Simulator! Adjust initial distortion delta, feedback exponent gamma, and citizen reporting baseline alpha. Watch how setting gamma such that T prime of one-half exceeds 1.0 triggers an irreversible supercritical pitchfork divergence, collapsing police allocations into a hundred percent enforcement trap in District A!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Look at the dynamical map canvas, Nova! When gamma is 1.80 and alpha is 0.20, T prime is 1.20, and District A patrol share escalates exponentially to ninety-nine percent! But as soon as I raise citizen reporting alpha to 0.40, T prime drops below one and parity is restored!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 1: In a predictive policing algorithm, citizen baseline reporting alpha is 0.333, and the feedback exponent gamma is 2.4. District A begins with a 2% initial reporting overcount. Calculate the derivative T prime of one-half and predict the long-term operational outcome. Select Option A, B, or C above me!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Alpha is 0.333, gamma is 2.4, and District A has a 2% initial bias! Review the three options above me and select the correct mathematical prediction!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Correct! T prime of one half equals gamma times one minus alpha divided by one plus alpha, which gives 2.4 times 0.50, exactly 1.20! Because 1.20 is strictly greater than 1.0, the parity fixed point is unstable. The initial 2% distortion undergoes runaway exponential divergence, allocating 100% of patrols to District A and manufacturing a synthetic crime wave!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Incorrect. The derivative formula at parity is gamma times one minus alpha over one plus alpha. Substituting 2.4 and 0.333 yields 1.20, which is strictly greater than 1.0! When the derivative exceeds one, the fixed point is repelling and unstable, driving the system to complete divergence rather than parity.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to the Fairness Trilemma and COMPAS Calibration Workbench! Observe Group 0 with base rate 32% and Group 1 with base rate 55%. Click Equalize PPV to inspect Northpointe's defense, or click Equalize FPR to see ProPublica's audit findings. Notice how equal calibration mathematically forces false positive disparity!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Look at the metric readouts, Nova! When we equalize positive predictive value, the calibration gap drops to zero, but the False Positive Rate disparity shoots up to 18 points! And when we equalize False Positive Rates, the Disparate Impact Ratio plunges to 0.65, violating the 80% rule!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Active Checkpoint 2: Group 0 has base rate 0.20, and Group 1 has base rate 0.50. An algorithm achieves equal positive predictive value and equal true positive rates across groups. What is the theoretical ratio of False Positive Rates, FPR zero over FPR one? Select Option A, B, or C above me!

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Base rates of 20% and 50% under equal calibration and opportunity! Review our three options above me and select the correct odds ratio!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Outstanding! By Kleinberg's Theorem, the ratio of False Positive Rates under equal calibration and opportunity equals the base rate odds ratio! Odds of p zero is 0.20 over 0.80, which is 0.25. Odds of p one is 0.50 over 0.50, which is 1.00. The ratio 0.25 over 1.00 equals exactly 0.25! Group zero's False Positive Rate is only 25% of Group one's rate, proving error rate parity is impossible!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Incorrect. Under Kleinberg's Theorem, the ratio of False Positive Rates is not the ratio of base rates, but the ratio of odds: p zero over 1 minus p zero divided by p one over 1 minus p one. Computing 0.25 divided by 1.00 yields 0.25.
